Thursday, 12 April 2035, in the evening, after the Thursday orchestra rehearsal. Julien, Isabelle and Sorina are talking about the day Viorica’s piano will return to the Maison Stan in Bucharest. Someone from Lyon has to be the first to play it.
Andrei has written again. The closer the date gets, the more he insists: someone from Lyon has to play the waltz on that piano.
Bertrand would play better than anyone, but he’s a violinist. We need a pianist.
Don’t look at me as if I were the only pianist in France!
You’re not the only one. But you’re Romanian, you’re from Lyon, and Viorica loves you as much as her own granddaughter.
Exactly. I’m all the more scared because I know her. I haven’t played in public for fifteen years.
You play every Thursday in front of thirty people.
It’s not the same thing as playing alone in front of a ninety-four-year-old lady who has been waiting for this moment since 1950.
The more you think about it, the less you feel like going. That’s normal. I used to get stage fright before every concert too.
And how did you get rid of it?
I didn’t get rid of it. I played as if nobody were listening to me, just as my neighbour used to whistle on the other side of the landing.
And besides, you won’t be alone. Rose-Hélène will come with the harmonica, as will the whole family.
(she sighs) All right. But I’m warning you: the more I rehearse, the more wrong notes I play.
So much the better. This waltz has never been played in tune. It’s all the more beautiful for it.

1. Plus… plus, moins… moins (correlatives)
For “the more… the more…”, French puts “plus” or “moins” at the start of EACH half, without “le” and without “que”:
Plus on attend, plus on a peur.
Moins il dort, moins il travaille bien.
The less he sleeps, the worse he works.
Plus tu y penses, moins tu as envie d’y aller.
The more you think about it, the less you feel like going.
Plus je répète, plus je fais de fausses notes.
The more I rehearse, the more wrong notes I play.

Typical mistake: “Le plus on attend, le plus on a peur” ✗ (copied from English) or “Plus on attend, que plus…” ✗. Correct: “Plus on attend, plus on a peur.” ✓. With “bon” and “bien”, use “meilleur / mieux”: “Plus il joue, mieux il joue.”
2. De plus en plus, de moins en moins
For gradual change (“more and more…”):
The piano sounds better and better.
Viorica goes out less and less.
There are more and more people in the street. (+ de + noun)
“De mieux en mieux” (better and better) and “de pire en pire” (worse and worse) are very common in speech.
3. D’autant plus que, d’autant moins que
“D’autant plus que” (all the more so as) adds a reason that STRENGTHENS the statement. It is a structure examiners appreciate in the DELF B2:
I’m all the more scared because I know her.
The piano sounds better, all the more so as the soundboard is new.
She feels all the less like leaving because it’s raining.
She is all the prouder of it. (without “que”, at the end)
Don’t confuse it with “surtout que” (informal). In writing, at B2, choose “d’autant plus que”.
4. Equality and similarity: autant que, le même que, de même que, ainsi que
as much as (with verbs)
Viorica t’aime autant que sa petite-fille.
as many… as
Il y avait autant de voisins que de musiciens.
le / la même… que
the same… as
Ce n’est pas la même chose que jouer seule.
de même que
De même que son père, elle aimait ce piano.
ainsi que
as well as, like
Rose-Hélène viendra, ainsi que toute la famille.
more (not followed by an adjective)
Elle l’aimait davantage chaque année.
“Davantage” usually comes at the end of the clause or before “de”: “davantage de temps”. Don’t say “davantage beau” ✗ → “plus beau” ✓.
5. Comme si + imperfect / pluperfect
“Comme si” (as if) introduces an unreal comparison. It is NOT followed by the conditional, but by the imperfect (same time) or the pluperfect (earlier time):
She played as if she were ten years old. (imperfect)
Don’t look at me as if I were the only pianist! (imperfect)
He smiled as if he had always known. (pluperfect)
The piano came back as if it had never left.
English speakers may be tempted by “would”: “comme si elle aurait dix ans” ✗. Correct: “comme si elle avait dix ans” ✓. Note: “si + il” → “s’il”.

Andrei’s message arrived on a Monday evening in April 2035, while Julien was doing the washing-up. It was shorter than usual, and all the clearer for it. Mr Petrescu had finished. Viorica’s piano would go back into the Maison Stan on Saturday 12 May, through the balcony window, the same way it had come out. And Viorica was asking, once again, for someone from Lyon to come and play the waltz on it.

They needed a pianist. Everyone thought of Sorina at the same moment, as if someone had said her name out loud. She was Romanian, she lived in Lyon, she played the piano every Thursday in Amina’s orchestra, and she was in love with Viorica’s grandson. Nobody could have imagined a better candidate. Nobody, except Sorina herself.

For Sorina had a secret she had told only Andrei. At nineteen, at the Cluj conservatory, she had played a Chopin ballade in front of a jury of five professors. In the middle of the piece, her hands had stopped. Just like that, all of a sudden, as if someone had cut the power. She had sat motionless in front of the keyboard for three minutes, in total silence. Then she had stood up and walked out.

The next day she had changed courses. She had become an architect, a good architect, more precise than most of her colleagues. But she had never again played alone in front of an audience. In the Thursday orchestra she hid behind the others, at the back of the hall, and the louder the piece, the calmer she felt. Nobody noticed her wrong notes among the trumpets.

And yet she said yes. One Thursday evening, after rehearsal, Julien and Isabelle had persuaded her, and she had ended up agreeing with a sigh. The next day she started rehearsing. Amina had given her the keys to the Salle Hélène Morel, and Sorina went there every evening after work, when there was nobody left. She played Henri’s waltz again and again on the hall’s old upright piano.

But the more she rehearsed, the more mistakes she made. At first she played one wrong note an evening. After a week she was playing ten. After two weeks her hands trembled as soon as she sat down. She knew the waltz by heart, better than anyone in Lyon, and yet she felt more and more as if she didn’t know how to play it.

One evening Rose-Hélène came to listen. She had turned seven on 4 March, and she could now read any book, even the ones without pictures. She sat in the front row, her harmonica in her hand, and said nothing during the whole waltz. At the end, Sorina asked her if it was really that terrible. Rose-Hélène thought about it with the seriousness of a grown-up.

She said Sorina played like someone afraid of waking a baby. Then she added that Grandma Odile used to play far more wrong notes than Sorina, and that this was exactly why everyone loved her so much. Nobody had ever asked her to whistle in tune. They had only asked her to whistle. Sorina laughed for the first time in two weeks.

From that evening on, Rose-Hélène came to the Salle Hélène Morel every evening, with her father or with Isabelle. She would sit in the front row and play the first three notes on the harmonica, and Sorina would answer on the piano. They played like that for three weeks. Strangely, when Rose-Hélène was the one who started, Sorina played far fewer wrong notes, as if she no longer had to decide on her own when to begin.

The following Thursday, Bertrand stayed behind after rehearsal. He listened to Sorina play, arms folded, without a word, the way he used to listen to accountants explaining their expenses. Then he told her he had stopped playing the violin for thirty-six years, and that he had been more afraid of picking up his bow again than of auditing any ministry.

He gave her a single piece of advice. You never play as badly as you fear, he said, nor as well as you hope. You always play somewhere in the middle, and that’s where people hear you. Sorina wrote the sentence down in her phone. Later she said that this advice had helped her more than fifteen years of piano lessons.

Meanwhile, Julien had received another call from Bucharest, a far more discreet one. It was Andrei again. He was speaking in a low voice, as if he were afraid Sorina might hear him all the way from Lyon. He wanted to ask Sorina to marry him. Not just anywhere, not just any time. On 12 May, at the Maison Stan, in front of his great-grandfather’s piano. And he needed help.

His idea was simple, and all the more beautiful because it came from the story itself. In 1950, Viorica’s father had hidden a letter under the piano keys, with the words: “For whoever opens this piano”. Andrei wanted to hide the ring in the same place, with a little note in his own hand: “For her who opens this piano”. It just had to be Sorina who opened it.

Julien promised to help him. He thought of the letter, which was still on show at the museum, in the display case opposite Odile’s armchair. Viorica wanted to put it back in the piano. If Sorina were the one to put it back, she would have to lift the board over the keys, and she would find the ring. The plan was perfect. Four people still had to be won over: Viorica, Mr Petrescu, Mrs Lacroix and Rose-Hélène, who had heard everything.

Viorica replied with a letter in violet ink, as always. She wrote that she was delighted. She added that the last time someone had hidden something in that piano, it had taken eighty-three years to find it. So she begged the young man to be a little quicker than his great-grandfather, since she no longer quite had the time to wait that long.

Mrs Lacroix, for her part, made a decision that surprised everyone. She announced that she would take the letter back to Bucharest herself. A copy would replace it in the display case until the end of the exhibition. She explained that such a precious document never travelled alone, and that a curator had to accompany it. Isabelle smiled. She knew Mrs Lacroix mostly wanted to hear the piano.

Finally, Rose-Hélène swore to keep the secret. She swore on Henri’s harmonica, which for her was the most serious oath there is. But a secret, at seven, is much heavier than a school bag. The more the days went by, the harder it was for her to carry. She avoided looking Sorina in the eye. She blushed whenever anyone said the word “piano”.

Mr Petrescu, on the other hand, grumbled on the phone for ten minutes. In fifty years in the trade he had never left anything inside a piano, not even a screw. A piano was not a letterbox. Then he remembered the 1950 letter, and he fell silent for a long moment. He ended up agreeing, on one condition: that the box be no bigger than a matchbox, so as not to spoil the sound.

At the same time, a video arrived from Dakar. Mariama had gone back there in April, as she had promised, to launch the Medina orchestra. It showed thirty-one children sitting under Lamine’s mango tree, with jerrycans, tin cans and three children’s violins sent by Gérard Thiébaut. They were playing the waltz. Or rather, they were playing something that vaguely resembled the waltz.

At the moment of silence, the thirty-one children had stopped all at once, perfectly, better than any professional orchestra. In the silence you could hear the crickets, a motorbike in the distance, and suddenly a goat bleating, right on the fifth bar. The children had burst out laughing. So had Lamine. Mariama, behind the camera, was shouting that the goat was now a member of the orchestra.

They left for Bucharest on Thursday 10 May, seven of them: Julien, Isabelle, Rose-Hélène, Henri-Ion, Sorina, Ioana and Mrs Lacroix, who held a small grey box on her knees, the way Bertrand used to hold his violin. In the box, between two sheets of special paper, was the 1950 letter. Mrs Lacroix didn’t let go of it once during the whole flight.

Henri-Ion, who was nearly five, asked questions non-stop. He wanted to know whether Bucharest was bigger than Lyon, whether Romanians whistled as well as people from Lyon, and whether the plane could fly faster than the waltz. Isabelle answered all the questions except the last. Rose-Hélène, sitting by the window, hardly said anything. She was guarding her secret.

At the airport, Andrei was waiting for them. He looked more nervous than a candidate before an exam. He kissed Sorina, then put his hand in his jacket pocket, as if to check that something was still there. Julien pretended not to see anything. Rose-Hélène looked at the pocket, then at Andrei, then at the pocket again, and turned bright red.

In the evening, Sorina’s mother invited them all to her home, a little house in the Cotroceni district. She had made sarmale for twenty people, though there were only eleven of them. Her name was Doina, she had been a primary teacher all her life, and she had paid for her daughter’s piano lessons by giving maths lessons on Sundays, for twelve years.

After dinner, Doina took out an old photo album. In it you could see Sorina at six, sitting at an upright piano too big for her, her feet dangling. Doina said that her daughter used to play as if the piano were a toy. Then one day, in Cluj, she had stopped playing, and Doina had never known why. Sorina looked at her mother. She had never told her.

She told her that evening, in the kitchen, while the others were having coffee in the living room. The jury, the ballade, the hands that stopped, the three minutes of silence. Doina listened without interrupting. Then she took her daughter’s hands in hers. She said she would have preferred to know fifteen years earlier, but that she was all the prouder to see her play on Saturday.

That night Sorina couldn’t sleep. Around two in the morning she got up without a sound and went into her old bedroom, where the old upright piano of her childhood was still there, under a pile of books. She played the waltz very softly, barely pressing the keys. She didn’t know that her mother, also awake, was listening in the corridor, sitting on the floor in her nightdress, as when Sorina was six.

On Friday morning, Ioana took them to visit the Maison Stan. Fabre & Popescu’s work had been finished for a month. The façade had got back its 1907 colours, cream and pale green. The great wave-shaped balcony, which had been dismantled to get the piano out, had been rebuilt identically by craftsmen from Sibiu. It was more beautiful than before, Viorica said, but she didn’t want to say it too loudly.

Inside there were twelve classrooms, all different, a small library and, on the first floor, the big drawing room where the piano used to stand. The parquet had been restored, board by board. Ilinca, Viorica’s granddaughter, had arrived from Madrid the day before. She would teach violin at the school from September. She had already chosen her room, the smallest, the one overlooking the garden.

In the afternoon they went to Mr Petrescu’s workshop, in a narrow street near the North Station. He was a small man of seventy, with a white moustache and astonishingly delicate hands. The workshop smelt of wood, glue and varnish. In the middle, under a large white sheet, was a shape everyone recognised at once.

Mr Petrescu pulled off the sheet slowly, the way a curtain rises in a theatre. The grand piano appeared, black and shining, much bigger than in the photos. Nobody spoke. Henri-Ion asked in a whisper whether it was the piano of the gentleman from 1950. Mr Petrescu replied that it was, but that it now had a new heart, made of Carpathian spruce.

He invited Sorina to try it. She approached it the way you approach an animal you don’t know. She put one finger on a key, then another. The keys were the original ones, of yellowed ivory, and each had a small hollow in the middle, where the fingers of Viorica’s father had pressed for thirty years. Sorina put her fingers exactly into those hollows. They were the same size as hers.

She played a chord. The sound filled the workshop, then the street, as if the piano had been waiting for this moment for years. It was softer than the piano in the Salle Hélène Morel, deeper, slower to fade. Sorina pulled her hands away as if she had burnt herself. She said she could never play on an instrument like that. Mr Petrescu smiled under his moustache.

He said he had heard that sentence hundreds of times, from pianists far more famous than she was. And that every time, the next day, they played. A piano, according to him, was not a judge. It was a friend with more patience than the others. The more you feared it, the quieter it became. The more you trusted it, the more it sang.

When Sorina went out into the courtyard with Isabelle, Andrei stayed in the workshop with Mr Petrescu and Julien. He took a small red box and a card folded in two out of his pocket. Mr Petrescu removed the board covering the keys with a tiny screwdriver, in two minutes. Andrei placed the box at the back, where the letter had slept for eighty-three years.

Rose-Hélène, who had come back for her harmonica, saw everything from the doorway. She said nothing. She just put a finger to her lips, very seriously, to show Andrei she knew how to keep a secret. Andrei made the same gesture. Then, like two conspirators, they went out into the courtyard together, where Sorina asked them why they looked so pleased.

On Saturday morning, the street behind Piața Romană had been closed to traffic. A yellow crane, taller than the house, was waiting in front of the façade. A lorry arrived at eight with the piano wrapped in grey blankets. Little by little the street filled up: neighbours, conservatory students, journalists, children, onlookers who didn’t know why they were there but who stayed.

Elena and Dan had come from Iași by train the day before. Grandma, who was eighty-nine, hadn’t been able to come, but Dan held his phone at arm’s length so she could watch everything live. Now and then her voice came out of the phone asking why it was taking so long, and whether people in Bucharest were still as slow as in her day.

Viorica was sitting on the balcony, in an armchair that had been put there for her, wrapped in a violet shawl. She was ninety-four. She had last seen this piano at home when she was ten, on the day in 1950 when her family had had to leave the house. She had sat at it for one last minute, played three notes, and then her father had taken her by the hand.

At nine o’clock the crane began to lift the piano. It rose slowly, very slowly, turning a little on itself, as if it were hesitating. The higher it rose, the quieter the street became. At the height of the first floor, all you could hear was the crane’s engine and Ioana’s orders as she directed the workers over the radio, in Romanian, in a voice calmer than ever.

It was then that a gust of wind swept through the street. The piano turned a quarter turn, then another, and swung dangerously close to the façade. The crowd cried out. Mr Petrescu went as white as his moustache. Ioana didn’t raise her voice. She said three words into the radio. Two workers pulled on the ropes, and the piano came to a stop twenty centimetres from the balcony.

The workers had removed the big balcony window the day before. The piano entered the house at nine forty-seven exactly, Ioana noted, as if it had never left. The whole street applauded. On the balcony, Viorica didn’t applaud. She just laid her hand on the black wood as it went by, the way you touch the shoulder of someone coming home from a very long journey.

In the drawing room they had to decide where to put it. Ioana had planned a spot near the window, brighter, more practical for concerts. But Viorica stood up, leaned on her cane and crossed the room. She stopped near the back wall. With the tip of her cane she pointed to three small marks in the parquet, three round hollows nobody had noticed.

They were the marks of the piano’s three legs. They had stayed there for eighty-five years, under the carpets of communist offices, then under the dust of neglect, then under the restorers’ varnish. The craftsmen from Sibiu had kept them without knowing what they were, because they thought it a shame to erase them. The workers set the piano exactly on top of them. The three legs went into the three hollows.

The drawing room gradually filled up. About sixty people could stand in it, and the windows were wide open onto the street, where several hundred more were waiting. Mrs Lacroix went up to Viorica with her little grey box. She opened it, took off her white gloves, which she never did, and handed her father’s letter back to her with bare hands.

Viorica reread the letter in silence, once again. Nobody knew exactly what it said, except her. She had always refused to read it aloud. She said she would put it back in the piano in a little while, after the waltz. Then she turned to Sorina and asked her, in Romanian, whether she was ready. Sorina said no. Viorica said that was perfect.

Sorina sat down on the stool. She put her hands on the keyboard, her fingers in the little ivory hollows. She looked at the room: sixty faces, raised phones, her mother in the front row, Mrs Lacroix, Andrei as white as a sheet. Through the windows she could hear the street waiting. And suddenly, exactly as in Cluj, her hands stopped.

They no longer moved. One second. Five seconds. Ten. The silence grew heavier and heavier, and the longer it lasted, the less Sorina could breathe. She thought she would get up and walk out, as fifteen years earlier. In the drawing room nobody dared move. Doina had her hands clasped. Andrei took a step towards the piano, then stopped, not knowing what to do.

It was Rose-Hélène who moved. She crossed the room without asking permission, sat down on the stool next to Sorina, very small, and took Henri’s harmonica out of her pocket. She said nothing. She played the first three notes of the waltz, softly, the way you knock on a door. Then she waited, exactly as Odile used to wait on the other side of the landing.

And Sorina’s hands answered. On their own, without her deciding. They played the next three notes, then the others, then the whole first verse. Sorina was no longer playing for a jury. She was playing as if she were six, in her mother’s kitchen in Cluj, feet dangling, on a piano too big for her. She was playing as if nobody were listening.

The piano sang. It sang better than in the workshop, all the more so as the drawing room, with its high ceiling, gave back the voice it had had in 1907. In the street, people fell silent. A tram passing at the end of the street slowed down. The driver, who had heard about the waltz on the radio, stopped his tram and opened the doors so the passengers could hear too.

Then came the third verse. Sorina lifted her hands. Silence fell over the drawing room, over the street, over the stopped tram. Eight bars. Several hundred people, in a Bucharest street, fell silent at the same time, without anyone having asked them. All you could hear were the pigeons on the roofs and, very far away, the noise of the city carrying on, as if it didn’t know.

On the fifth bar, Viorica stood up. Andrei wanted to help her, but she refused with a gesture. She crossed the room with her cane, slowly, and stopped beside Sorina. She held out a single finger, the index finger of her right hand, and played three notes. The next three notes of the waltz. At exactly the right moment, neither too early nor too late.

She had not touched this piano for eighty-five years. She played those three notes as if she were still ten, as if her father were still behind her, his hand on her shoulder. Then she stepped back, and Sorina took up the waltz where Viorica had left it. She played it to the end without a single wrong note. Which, Julien said later, was almost a pity.

When the last note faded, there was a moment of silence longer than the eight bars. Then the street exploded. People clapped, whistled, shouted. In the tram, the passengers banged on the windows. And out of Dan’s phone came the small voice of an old lady whistling the three notes, off-key, louder than everyone. Grandma had insisted on answering too.

Sorina was crying without realising it. Viorica handed her her father’s letter. She asked her, in Romanian, to put it back in the piano herself, in its place, for the next person who would open it. Mr Petrescu stepped forward with his tiny screwdriver. He removed the board over the keys and stepped back. The whole room was watching. Rose-Hélène put both hands over her mouth.

Sorina leaned over to slip the letter in at the back. Her hand stopped. There was already something there. A small red box, and a card folded in two. She opened the card. She recognised Andrei’s slanting handwriting at once. There were only a few words: “For her who opens this piano”. She looked up. Andrei was no longer in his place.

He was on his knees, next to the stool, among the sixty people and the raised phones. He had prepared a long speech, in French and Romanian, with lots of comparisons. He said only the first sentence: “The more I know you, the more I want to know you.” Then he forgot all the rest, and simply asked whether she would.

Sorina laughed and cried at the same time. She said yes in Romanian, then in French, then in Romanian again, as if one language weren’t enough. Doina sat down on the nearest chair. In the street, those who had seen nothing applauded anyway, because those who had seen were applauding. And Rose-Hélène shouted, louder than everyone, that she had kept the secret for twenty-six hours.

Viorica took the letter from Sorina’s hands, since Sorina no longer quite knew what she was doing. She slipped it in at the back of the piano herself, next to the empty spot where the little red box had been. Mr Petrescu screwed the board back on. Viorica said that this time the letter would have company, and that the next person to open the piano would find two stories instead of one.

Indeed, Andrei had left the card. Sorina had put the ring on her finger, but she had wanted the card to stay in the piano, next to the 1950 letter. Underneath, in pencil, she had written the date and a single word: “Yes”. Mrs Lacroix, who had witnessed the whole scene, said no museum in the world would ever own such a precious document, and that she was almost jealous.

In the evening there was a dinner in the garden of the Maison Stan, under the lime trees that had not yet flowered. Doina had made sarmale again, for forty people this time. Ilinca played the violin. Mr Petrescu told the story of the gust of wind at least six times, and each time the piano came a little closer to the façade. By the end, it had almost touched it.

Ioana, sitting next to Sorina, made her an offer over dessert. Fabre & Popescu was going to open an office in Bucharest, for restoration projects in Romania. Someone was needed to run it. Someone who knew both countries, both languages, and old houses. Sorina looked at Andrei, then at Ioana, then at her mother. She said she needed a night to think about it. She said yes before the coffee.

During dinner, Grandma called again from Iași, on Dan’s phone. She wanted to speak to Sorina. She told her she had whistled louder than the whole of Bucharest, and that this was only natural, because people from Moldavia had better lungs than people from the capital. Then she demanded to be invited to the wedding. And she added that it would be more sensible to hold it in Iași, since she was older than everyone and no longer travelled.

Later, Rose-Hélène sat down next to Viorica on a garden bench. She asked her whether the piano was better than before, when she was little. Viorica thought for a long time. Then she said the piano was like her. The older it got, the less in tune it played, and the more people loved it. Rose-Hélène said it was exactly like Grandma Odile. Viorica said she had suspected as much.

She added that all those years she had been afraid the piano had forgotten her. That it wouldn’t recognise her any more. But earlier, when she had put her finger on the key, it had answered exactly as in 1950, as if she had never left. Pianos, she said, have better memories than people. Just like lime trees, replied Rose-Hélène, who knew a thing or two about that.

That night, when everyone had left, Andrei walked Viorica back to the drawing room, because she wanted to see the piano once more before going to sleep. She sat down at it, alone, in the dark. And she played, with two fingers, very slowly, the Chopin waltz her father had taught her in 1949. She made four mistakes. She carried on all the same.

The windows had been left open. Across the street, in a block of flats from the sixties, a light came on on the third floor. Someone leaned out of the window. They listened to the end. Then, in the Bucharest night, they whistled three notes. It wasn’t Chopin. It was Henri’s waltz. Viorica smiled in the dark. She answered with one finger.

The music school at the Maison Stan would open on Monday 3 September 2035, with a hundred and twenty pupils enrolled, a waiting list longer than the street, and twelve teachers. There would be piano, violin and singing lessons, and even kora, thanks to Lamine, who would come one week a year. In the big drawing room on the first floor, the grand piano would wait, on its three hollows, for the children to come and open it.

And Sorina would play in public again. Not often, not in front of juries, not Chopin ballades. But on the first Saturday of every month, at ten o’clock, she would play Henri’s waltz on the Maison Stan piano, with the windows open onto the street. The more time passed, the more people there would be under the windows. And at the third verse, every time, the whole street would fall silent for eight bars.

Reading: The restoration report

The report that Mr Petrescu, the piano restorer, wrote for the Maison Stan foundation. Notice how he compares the piano “before” and “after”. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Rapport de restauration : piano à queue, Maison Stan
When the piano arrived in my workshop in September 2033, it was in a far worse state than I had imagined. The soundboard was cracked, the keyboard yellowed, and several keys no longer responded.
The more I dismantled it, the more damage I discovered. Seventy-five years of neglect is longer than the life of most instruments. And yet the walnut case was as solid as on the first day.

I replaced the soundboard with a new one, made of Carpathian spruce, as well as the strings and hammers. On the other hand, I kept the original keys, all the more so as you can still see on them the wear of the first owner’s fingers.

Today the sound is clearer than before, but less brilliant than that of a modern piano. That is intentional. An old piano must not sound as if it had just come out of a factory. It must sound as if it remembered.
This work took me two years instead of the six months planned. The more the piano found its voice again, the less I wanted to give it back. I admit it: I tuned it three times more than necessary.
I thank Mrs Viorica Stan for her patience, as well as the firm Fabre & Popescu. This piano is not as perfect as a new one. It is better: it has a story. — Mihai Petrescu, restorer
